analysis.one_liner: Bans health insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, and drug wholesalers from also owning doctor practices, pharmacies, or other providers, forcing them to sell one side off.
analysis.headline: The Break Up Big Medicine Act, which would force health conglomerates to sell off their medical providers, was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote since February 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for health insurers, pharmacy benefit managers (the middlemen that decide which drugs are covered and what pharmacies get paid), and large drug and medical device wholesalers to also own doctor practices, pharmacies, hospitals, or clinics. Any company caught on both sides of that line would have one year to sell off one side of its business, with federal and state enforcers — and individual patients — able to sue to make it happen. The bill was just introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, patients would benefit from rules that stop insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, and drug wholesalers from owning the doctors, pharmacies, and clinics they steer patients toward; the bill's findings cite FTC findings that such steering raises drug costs and cite Medicare Advantage plans using employed physicians to generate inflated federal payments. Independent physicians and pharmacies would gain competitors' protection, since they now face conglomerates that own both the plan and the provider. Taxpayers would gain from reduced incentive to inflate Medicare billing, and a private right of action with triple damages would let individuals and state attorneys general sue violators, with disgorged revenue funding health needs in harmed communities [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, taxpayers, independent doctors and pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: It outlaws the common ownership of health insurers or pharmacy benefit managers with medical providers and management services organizations, and of drug and device wholesalers with providers, directly targeting the vertical integration the bill's findings describe.

It requires violators to divest one side of the business within one year, with monthly escrow of 10 percent of profits, a court-appointed trustee who can force a sale, and FTC/DOJ review of every divestiture and subsequent acquisition.

It gives patients and state attorneys general the power to sue, with triple damages and attorney's fees for prevailing individuals, and requires money disgorged from violators to be spent on health care needs in the harmed communities.

It targets the specific harms named in its findings: PBM self-preferencing that raises drug costs, insurers steering enrollees to affiliated doctors, gaming of medical loss ratio profit limits, inflated Medicare Advantage payments generated by employed physicians, and wholesalers steering specialists toward the most lucrative drugs and devices.

analysis.who_pays: Large vertically integrated health companies would bear the cost: parent companies that own an insurer or a pharmacy benefit manager would have to divest every medical provider and management services organization they own, and drug and medical device wholesalers would have to divest the medical practices they have been acquiring. Companies that miss the one-year divestment deadline would have 10 percent of their profits moved into escrow each month and could have their provider businesses sold off by a court-appointed trustee [S2].

drawbacks.text: A one-year divestment deadline for companies that own roughly 10 percent of American physicians, nearly 80 percent of PBM claims processing, and 98 percent of drug distribution could disrupt continuity of care while provider businesses are sold or reorganized, leaving patients briefly uncertain who employs or owns their doctor or pharmacy.

The bill forces divestment but cannot control who buys the divested practices; without further conditions, provider businesses cut loose from one conglomerate could be acquired by private equity firms or another large company, reproducing corporate ownership under a different name.

Its remedies are unusually aggressive — automatic monthly escrow of 10 percent of a company's profits and trustee-forced sales — and critics would argue this exceeds the penalties conventional antitrust law imposes even for provable violations, raising questions about proportionality and administrability.
The bill addresses ownership structure, not prices directly; it does not cap drug prices or insurer premiums, so any savings to patients depend on restored competition actually materializing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential upside is large: the bill attacks the specific conflicts of interest — steering, profit-shifting around regulatory caps, and inflated Medicare payments — that its findings document with FTC evidence, and it backs the mandate with real enforcement teeth, including private lawsuits and a fund for harmed communities. The main costs are the transition risk of a one-year breakup of some of the largest companies in America, the possibility that divested practices simply change hands to other large owners, and remedies that some would call disproportionate. The bill does nothing about prices directly, so its benefits to patients are indirect and depend on competition returning.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has not taken it up, so it is sitting there awaiting action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 10, 2026, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
Since that referral, no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — appears in the bill's action history.
The bill had one cosponsor, Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, a Republican, alongside its Democratic sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the large vertically integrated health conglomerates. No committee has acted on the bill, so no insurer, pharmacy benefit manager, or wholesaler faces any divestment requirement, and the consolidation the bill describes continues as is.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Break Up Big Medicine Act to require structural separation of insurers, PBMs, and wholesalers from medical providers.

for.name: Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship as its sole Republican cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat introduced the bill and one of 55 Senate Republicans cosponsored it, but no votes have occurred, so no partisan pattern is established.

industries.note: The bill would force insurers and their PBM affiliates to divest the physician practices, clinics, and pharmacies they own or control through management services organizations, ending their ability to steer patients to in-house providers and, per the bill's findings, to shift profits around the medical loss ratio cap. This targets the business model of the largest national insurers.

The bill's core prohibition covers PBMs under common ownership with providers and insurers, breaking up the three PBM giants that process nearly 80 percent of prescription drug claims and that the FTC found steer business to their own pharmacies.

industries.industry: Prescription drug and medical device wholesalers
industries.note: Wholesalers that have acquired specialty medical practices — about $16 billion in acquisitions across 35 states since January 2024, per the bill's findings — would have to divest those providers and could no longer steer specialists toward their most lucrative drugs and devices.

With more than three-quarters of American doctors employed by corporate entities per the bill's findings, separating providers from insurers and wholesalers would remove the steering pressure that pushes patients to affiliated practices and give independent practices a fairer market.
Community and independent pharmacies currently compete against PBM-owned pharmacies that the FTC found receive steered business; structural separation would end that conflict of interest.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to Senate committee without further action rarely reach the floor, and structural divestiture bills of this scale have historically not advanced even with bipartisan sponsorship; unless it gains more cosponsors or is attached to a larger package, it is likely to sit in committee until the Congress ends.
